questions.question: Which factor has contributed most to the depletion of high-grade mineral ores in India over recent decades?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Selective mining of rich ores**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Selective mining**, often referred to as **"high-grading"** or **"picking the eyes"** of a mine, involves the extraction of only the highest-grade mineral ores from a deposit while ignoring or discarding lower-grade ores. This practice has been the primary driver for the rapid depletion of high-quality mineral resources in **India** over the **last few decades**.
 
• Miners often prioritize **high-grade ores** because they require less processing, involve lower **refining costs**, and fetch **higher market prices** immediately, thereby maximizing **short-term profits**.
 
• In the context of **India**, this practice has significantly affected reserves of **Iron Ore (Hematite)** and **Manganese**. For example, during the **mining boom** in states like **Goa** and **Karnataka**, selective extraction was rampant to meet the sudden surge in **international demand**.
 
• The **Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM)** and the **Ministry of Mines** have noted that selective mining leads to the **sterilization of minerals**. When only the rich pockets are extracted, the remaining low-grade ore often becomes **economically unviable** or technically difficult to recover later, leading to a permanent loss of potential **national wealth**.
 
• By focusing solely on the "rich" portions, the **life of the mine** is drastically shortened. This unsustainable approach contradicts the principles of **mineral conservation** as outlined in the **Mineral Conservation and Development Rules (MCDR)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Iron Ore Reserves in India:** India is endowed with large reserves of iron ore, primarily **Hematite** and **Magnetite**. **Hematite** is considered high-grade (containing **60% to 70% metallic iron**) and is found extensively in **Odisha**, **Jharkhand**, and **Chhattisgarh**. **Magnetite**, though of lower grade (approx. **62% iron** but with more impurities), is found in **Karnataka** and **Andhra Pradesh**.
 
• **Mineral Export Policy:** India has historically been a major **exporter** of iron ore, particularly to **China**, **Japan**, and **South Korea**. The **increased export of unprocessed minerals** (Option 3) certainly impacts the **availability** for domestic industries, but **selective mining** is the root cause for the **physical depletion** of the highest-grade deposits.
 
• **Geological Distribution:** Most of India's metallic minerals are concentrated in the **Peninsular Plateau** region within ancient crystalline rocks. The **North-Eastern Plateau Region** (covering **Chhota Nagpur**) is the richest mineral belt, housing **coal**, **iron ore**, and **manganese**.
 
• **Legislative Framework:** The **Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act)** is the principal legislation governing the mining sector. Recent amendments in **2015** and **2021** introduced **e-auctions** for mineral blocks to ensure **transparency** and encourage **scientific mining** practices rather than selective extraction.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **National Mineral Policy (2019):** This policy emphasizes **sustainable mining** and the **"Zero Waste"** mining goal. It encourages the use of **beneficiation technologies** to upgrade **low-grade ores** so they can be blended with high-grade ores, reducing the pressure on high-grade reserves.
 
• **Impact of Overdependence on Coal:** While **coal-based industries** (Option 2) are massive in India, they contribute more to **environmental pollution** and **carbon emissions** rather than the direct depletion of high-grade **metallic mineral ores**.
 
• **Foreign Investment:** Contrary to Option 1, **India** has opened **100% FDI** (Foreign Direct Investment) in the mining sector under the **automatic route** for many minerals to bring in **advanced technology** that can handle low-grade ores efficiently.
 
• **Statistics:** India ranks **4th** in the world in terms of **Iron Ore production**. In the **year 2022-23**, the production of iron ore was approximately **250 million tonnes**, with **Odisha** contributing more than **50%** of the total output.

⇒ Present sum = 20 + 9 = 29

⇒ x + 2x + (x − 3) = 29

questions.question: According to Article 171 of the Constitution of India, the total membership of a State’s Legislative Council shall not surpass which of the following proportions of the total members of the State Legislative Assembly?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**One-third**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to **Article 171** of the **Constitution of India**, the total number of members in the **Legislative Council** of a State shall not exceed **one-third** of the total number of members in the **Legislative Assembly** of that State.
 
• The **Article 171(1)** further specifies that while there is an upper limit based on the Assembly's strength, the total number of members in the **Legislative Council** shall in no case be less than **40**.
 
• The **Legislative Council** (also known as the **Vidhan Parishad**) serves as the **Upper House** of a State's legislature, functioning similarly to the **Rajya Sabha** at the Union level.
 
• The composition of the Council is diverse: **one-third** of members are elected by **municipalities, district boards**, and other **local authorities**; **one-twelfth** are elected by **graduates** of three years' standing; **one-twelfth** are elected by **teachers**; and **one-third** are elected by the members of the **Legislative Assembly**.
 
• The remaining members (approximately **one-sixth**) are nominated by the **Governor** from among persons having special knowledge or practical experience in fields such as **Literature, Science, Art, Cooperative Movement, and Social Service**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• As of **2024**, only **six states** in India have a **bicameral legislature**, meaning they possess both a Legislative Assembly and a Legislative Council. These states are **Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, and Uttar Pradesh**.
 
• Under **Article 169** of the **Constitution**, the **Parliament** has the power to **create or abolish** a **Legislative Council** in a state if the **Legislative Assembly** of that state passes a resolution to that effect by a **special majority**.
 
• A **special majority** implies a majority of the **total membership** of the Assembly and a majority of not less than **two-thirds** of the members **present and voting**.
 
• The **Legislative Council** is a **permanent body** and is not subject to **dissolution**, unlike the Legislative Assembly which has a fixed term of **5 years** unless dissolved earlier.
 
• The tenure of a member of the **Legislative Council (MLC)** is **six years**, with **one-third** of the members retiring every **two years**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• To be eligible for membership in the **Legislative Council**, a person must be a **citizen of India**, must be at least **30 years of age**, and must be a **voter** in the relevant state.
 
• The **Legislative Council** has significantly less power than the **Legislative Assembly**; for example, it cannot **reject or amend** a **Money Bill** and can only delay it for a maximum of **14 days**.
 
• In the case of **Ordinary Bills**, the Council can delay a bill for a maximum of **four months** (three months in the first instance and one month in the second instance), after which the bill is deemed passed if the Assembly insists.
 
• The **Chairman** and the **Deputy Chairman** of the Council are elected by the **members** from among themselves to preside over the proceedings of the House.
 
• Currently, **Union Territories** like **Delhi, Puducherry, and Jammu & Kashmir** have **Legislative Assemblies**, but none of them have a **Legislative Council**.

questions.question: What are the three aims of economic policy listed in the 1991 document?

options.text: Market Liberalisation, Trade Restrictions, State Control

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Liberalisation, Globalisation, Privatisation**__.

__
 
• The **New Economic Policy (NEP)** was formally launched in **July 1991** by the **Government of India** to address a severe economic crisis. It shifted the economic strategy from a state-led model to a market-driven model.
 
• **Liberalisation**: This aimed at ending the **"License Raj"** by removing unnecessary **government restrictions** and **regulations** on industrial activity. It included the abolition of **industrial licensing** for most sectors and the relaxation of the **MRTP Act (Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act)**. ***Hence, the mention of Liberalisation in option 2 is correct.***
 
• **Privatisation**: This involved reducing the dominance of the **public sector** by transferring ownership or management of **Government-owned enterprises** to the **private sector**. A key tool used was **disinvestment**, where the government sold its **equity** in **Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)**. ***Hence, the mention of Privatisation in option 2 is correct.***
 
• **Globalisation**: This aimed at integrating the **Indian economy** with the **global economy**. It involved reducing **import duties**, allowing **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)**, and making the **Indian Rupee** partially convertible to encourage **international trade**. ***Hence, the mention of Globalisation in option 2 is correct.***
 
• **Option 1 (Protectionism, Regulation, Public Ownership)**: These were the hallmarks of the pre-1991 era, characterized by high **tariffs** and state control, which the **1991 document** sought to replace. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Context of 1991 Reforms**: The reforms were initiated under the leadership of **Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao** and **Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh**. The primary trigger was a **Balance of Payments (BoP)** crisis where **foreign exchange reserves** had dropped to a level barely enough to cover **two weeks** of imports.
 
• **Role of International Organizations**: To manage the crisis, **India** approached the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** and the **World Bank** for a loan of **$7 billion**. These organizations mandated structural reforms, leading to the adoption of the **LPG model**.
 
• **Industrial Policy 1991**: This policy drastically reduced the number of industries reserved for the **public sector** from **17** to just **8** (which has been further reduced over the years to sectors like **Railways** and **Atomic Energy**).
 
• **Impact on Trade**: The **1991 document** paved the way for **export promotion** instead of just **import substitution**. It led to the establishment of the **World Trade Organization (WTO)** framework in **India** by **1995**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Nationalisation (Option 3)**: This was a major theme in the **1960s** and **1970s**, most notably the **nationalisation of 14 major commercial banks** in **1969** and **6 more** in **1980**. The **1991 reforms** moved in the opposite direction. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• **Trade Restrictions (Option 4)**: The **1991 policy** specifically aimed to **dismantle trade restrictions** like **quotas** and high **customs duties** to make **Indian industries** globally competitive. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• **Economic Indicators**: Following the **1991 reforms**, India's **GDP growth rate** increased significantly, reaching over **6-7%** in the subsequent decades, and **Foreign Exchange Reserves** grew from approximately **$1.2 billion** in **June 1991** to over **$600 billion** in recent years.
 
• **Key Legislation**: The **Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA)** replaced the more restrictive **FERA (Foreign Exchange Regulation Act)** in **1999** to facilitate **external trade** and payments, aligning with the **Globalisation** goal.

options.text: UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)

• The **Global Methane Status Report** is a flagship publication released by the **UN Environment Programme (UNEP)**, particularly through its **International Methane Emissions Observatory (IMEO)**. In **2025**, this report provides a critical update on the progress made toward the **Global Methane Pledge**.
 
• The report serves as a primary monitoring tool to track whether the world is on path to reduce **methane emissions** by **30%** from **2020 levels** by the year **2030**. This target is essential for limiting global warming to **1.5°C**.
 
• It utilizes high-resolution data from **satellite technology** and the **Methane Alert and Response System (MARS)** to identify **super-emitters** and large-scale leaks in the **energy sector**.
 
• Methane is highlighted in the report as being responsible for approximately **30%** of the rise in **global temperatures** since the **Industrial Revolution**, making its mitigation a high priority for **UNEP**.
 
• The **2025** report emphasizes the **oil and gas**, **agriculture**, and **waste** sectors as the largest contributors to anthropogenic methane, providing **country-specific data** to guide policy interventions. ***Hence, the correct answer is UN Environment Programme (UNEP).***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **UN Environment Programme (UNEP):**

 
 
• Established on **June 5, 1972**, following the **Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment**.
 
• Headquartered in **Nairobi, Kenya**, it is the leading global environmental authority that sets the global environmental agenda.
 
• Its **Executive Director** (as of recent terms) is **Inger Andersen**. It coordinates responses to **climate change**, **biodiversity loss**, and **pollution**.
 
 
 
• **World Meteorological Organization (WMO):**
 
 
• Founded in **1950** and headquartered in **Geneva, Switzerland**.
 
• It is a specialized agency of the **United Nations** for **meteorology**, **operational hydrology**, and **geophysical sciences**.
 
• While it publishes the annual **Greenhouse Gas Bulletin**, it focuses more on atmospheric concentrations rather than the specific **Global Methane Status Report**.
 
 
 
• **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC):**
 
 
• Established in **1988** by the **WMO** and **UNEP**.
 
• It provides regular **Scientific Assessments** (such as **AR6** or **AR7**) regarding climate change but does not usually release annual status reports on specific gases like methane.
 
 
 
• **UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC):**
 
 
• Adopted in **1992** at the **Rio Earth Summit**, it is the parent treaty of the **2015 Paris Agreement**.
 
• It facilitates the **Conference of the Parties (COP)** meetings, where **global methane** targets are negotiated, though technical reporting is often delegated to **UNEP**.

• **Methane Characteristics:** Methane (**CH4**) has a **Global Warming Potential (GWP)** that is over **80 times** more potent than **carbon dioxide (CO2)** over a **20-year period**. Because it is short-lived in the atmosphere (about **12 years**), reducing it offers immediate cooling benefits.
 
• **Global Methane Pledge:** Launched at **COP26** in **Glasgow (2021)**, led by the **United States** and the **European Union**. More than **150 countries** have joined this voluntary commitment.
 
• **IMEO (International Methane Emissions Observatory):** Launched by **UNEP** with support from the **European Commission** to provide a public database of **empirically verified methane emissions**.

• **Puducherry** (formerly known as **Pondicherry**) is a **Union Territory** that possesses its own **Legislative Assembly** and a **Council of Ministers** to assist and advise the **Lieutenant Governor**. This provision was enabled by the **14th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962**, which inserted **Article 239A** into the **Constitution of India**. ***Hence, the statement regarding Puducherry having a legislature is correct.***

• **Daman and Diu** and **Dadra and Nagar Haveli** were previously separate **Union Territories** without their own legislatures. They were merged into a single entity known as the **Union Territory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu** on **January 26, 2020**. This combined territory is administered directly by the **President** through an **Administrator** and does not have a **Legislative Assembly**. ***Hence, the statement regarding these territories having a legislature is incorrect.***
 
• The **Andaman and Nicobar Islands** is an island territory located in the **Bay of Bengal**. It is categorized as a **Union Territory** without a legislature and is administered by a **Lieutenant Governor** appointed by the **President of India**. Decisions for the islands are made through the **Home Ministry** and the **Presidential** regulations under **Article 240**. ***Hence, the statement regarding Andaman and Nicobar Islands having a legislature is incorrect.***

• **Constitutional Provisions for Union Territories:** **Part VIII** of the **Constitution of India** (**Articles 239 to 241**) deals with the administration of **Union Territories**. While some **UTs** are directly administered by the **President** through an **Administrator**, others like **Delhi**, **Puducherry**, and **Jammu & Kashmir** have been provided with a **Legislative Assembly** and a **Council of Ministers** due to their specific administrative and political needs.
 
• **The Case of Delhi:** The **National Capital Territory of Delhi** was provided with a **Legislative Assembly** and a **Council of Ministers** through the **69th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991**, which added **Article 239AA**. Unlike **Puducherry**, **Delhi's** assembly has restricted powers over subjects like **Public Order**, **Police**, and **Land**, which remain under the **Central Government**.
 
• **Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization:** Following the **Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization Act, 2019**, the former state was bifurcated into two **Union Territories**: **Jammu & Kashmir** (with a legislature) and **Ladakh** (without a legislature). This change came into effect on **October 31, 2019**.
 
• **Difference in Administration:** In **Union Territories** like **Chandigarh** or **Lakshadweep**, the **Administrator** (often an **IAS officer** or a political appointee) holds the executive power. In **UTs** with a legislature, the **Lieutenant Governor** (**LG**) acts as the **Constitutional Head**, but the **Council of Ministers** headed by the **Chief Minister** exercises executive powers on most state subjects.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

questions.question: Three bells ring at regular intervals. The first bell rings every 120 minutes, the second every 180 minutes, and the third every 240 minutes. If all three bells ring together at 9:00 a.m., at what time will they ring together again?

Find LCM of 120, 180, 240

120 = 2³ × 3 × 5

180 = 2² × 3² × 5

240 = 2⁴ × 3 × 5

LCM = 2⁴ × 3² × 5 = 720 min = 12 hrs

9:00 a.m. + 12 hrs = 9:00 p.m.

**∴ Answer = 9:00 p.m.**

⇒ 240 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 5

⇒ Let sin²θ = x

⇒ x + 1/x = 10/3

• **Nucleic acids** are the **biomolecules** that include **Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA)** and **Ribonucleic Acid (RNA)**. These are considered the primary **information-carrying molecules** in all living organisms and viruses.
 
• Chemically, **nucleic acids** are **biopolymers**, or large **biomolecules**, essential for all known forms of life. They are composed of monomers called **nucleotides**.
 
• Each **nucleotide** is made of three components: a **five-carbon sugar (pentose)**, a **phosphate group**, and a **nitrogenous base**. The identity of the nucleic acid is determined by the sugar; **DNA** contains **deoxyribose**, while **RNA** contains **ribose**.
 
• The main **function** of these molecules is the **storage and expression** of **genomic information**. DNA acts as the master blueprint for life, while RNA is responsible for translating that genetic code into **functional proteins**.
 
• **Friedrich Miescher** first discovered nucleic acids in **1869** when he isolated a substance he called **'nuclein'** from the nuclei of human white blood cells.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Proteins**: These are complex **biomolecules** made up of long chains of **amino acids**. They perform a vast array of **functions** within organisms, including **catalyzing metabolic reactions (enzymes)**, **DNA replication**, and providing **structural support** (like **collagen** in skin and **keratin** in hair). They are encoded by the **genes** found in nucleic acids.
 
• **Lipids**: This class of **biomolecules** includes **fats, oils, waxes, and certain vitamins (like A, D, E, and K)**. They are **hydrophobic** (water-fearing) and serve as **energy storage** molecules, structural components of **cell membranes (phospholipids)**, and important **signaling molecules (hormones)**.
 
• **Carbohydrates**: Often referred to as **saccharides**, these are **organic compounds** composed of **carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen**. Their primary **application** is as a major **energy source** for the body. Examples include **glucose (monosaccharide)** used for immediate energy, **glycogen** for energy storage in animals, and **cellulose** which provides structural strength to **plant cell walls**.
 
• **Nitrogenous Bases**: In **DNA**, the bases are **Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), and Thymine (T)**. In **RNA**, **Thymine** is replaced by **Uracil (U)**. These bases follow specific **base-pairing rules** (A with T/U, and C with G), which allow for the accurate **replication** of genetic material.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **DNA Structure**: In **1953**, **James Watson** and **Francis Crick** proposed the **double helix** model of **DNA**, which describes two strands of nucleotides winding around each other. This structure is stabilized by **hydrogen bonds** between the nitrogenous bases.
 
• **RNA Types**: There are three main types of **RNA** involved in **protein synthesis**: **Messenger RNA (mRNA)**, which carries the genetic code from DNA; **Transfer RNA (tRNA)**, which brings amino acids to the ribosome; and **Ribosomal RNA (rRNA)**, which makes up the physical structure of **ribosomes**.
 
• **Central Dogma**: This is the fundamental framework of **molecular biology** that explains the flow of genetic information: **DNA** is transcribed into **RNA**, and **RNA** is translated into **Protein**. This process is universal to almost all **living organisms**.
 
• **Modern Applications**: The study of nucleic acids has led to breakthroughs like the **Human Genome Project** (completed in **2003**), **DNA fingerprinting** for **forensic science**, **PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)** for disease testing, and the development of **mRNA vaccines** (notably used during the **COVID-19 pandemic**).

questions.question: A shopkeeper fixes the marked price of an item 100% above its cost price. What percentage of discount on marked price should be allowed to gain 26%?
questions.solution:

Let CP = 100 ⇒ MP = 200 (100% above)

Required SP for 26% profit = 126

Discount = 200 − 126 = 74

Discount % = (74 / 200) × 100 = 37%

**∴ Answer = 37%**

⇒ Profit = 26%

⇒ MP = CP + 100% of CP

⇒ SP = CP + 26% of CP

⇒ Discount % = (MP − SP) / MP × 100

**Calculations:**

⇒ Let CP = 100

⇒ MP = 100 + 100 = 200

⇒ SP = 100 + 26 = 126

⇒ Discount = 200 − 126 = 74

⇒ Discount % = (74 / 200) × 100 = 37%

questions.question: According to the World Population Review Report, 2024, which of the following regions of the world has the highest population density?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**South-Central Asia**__.

__
 
• According to the **World Population Review Report 2024**, the region of **South-Central Asia** remains one of the most densely populated areas in the world due to its high concentration of people in countries like **India**, **Pakistan**, and **Bangladesh**.
 
• **South-Central Asia** exhibits a high population density primarily because it contains some of the world's most fertile lands, such as the **Indo-Gangetic Plain**, which supports large-scale **agriculture** and **urban settlements**.
 
• **Bangladesh**, a key country in this region, is frequently cited as the most densely populated non-city-state nation, with a density reaching over **1,100 to 1,300 people per square kilometer** in **2024**.
 
• The high density in this region is also driven by rapid **urbanization** and a historically high **total fertility rate**, although these rates have been stabilizing in recent years.
 
• Comparing the options, **Central Africa** and **North America** have significantly lower densities because they possess vast areas of **forests**, **deserts**, or **tundra** that are sparsely inhabited, while **Western Europe** is dense but does not match the sheer volume of **South-Central Asia**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Western Europe**: This region includes countries like **Germany**, **France**, and the **Netherlands**. While the **Netherlands** is very dense, the regional average is lower than **South-Central Asia** due to stable **population growth** and varied **land use**.
 
• **Central Africa**: Despite having a high **birth rate**, this region has a lower population density because of its massive **geographic area** covered by the **Congo Basin rainforests**, which limits human settlement density.
 
• **North America**: This region, comprising the **USA** and **Canada**, has one of the lowest population densities globally, averaging around **15 to 20 people per square kilometer**, largely because of the vast, unpopulated northern territories of **Canada** and the **Western United States**.
 
• **Population Density** is a measurement of population per unit area, typically expressed as **persons per square kilometer**. It is a crucial **demographic index** used by organizations like the **United Nations** and the **World Bank** to plan **infrastructure** and **resource allocation**.
 
• As of **2024**, the **global average population density** (excluding Antarctica) is estimated to be approximately **60 people per square kilometer**, showing a steady increase over the **last decade**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **India's Role**: In **2023**, **India** officially became the most populous country in the world, surpassing **China**. This shift has further cemented **South-Central Asia** as the highest density hub in the **2024** reports.
 
• **Microstates**: While **South-Central Asia** is the densest **region**, the highest density **locations** globally are actually microstates like **Monaco**, **Singapore**, and **Macau**, where density can exceed **19,000 people per square kilometer**.
 
• **Historical Context**: The density of **South-Central Asia** has been high for centuries due to the **favorable climate** and **river systems** like the **Ganges**, **Indus**, and **Brahmaputra**, which allowed for the early development of **civilizations**.
 
• **Economic Impact**: High population density in regions like **South-Central Asia** creates a massive **labor market** and **consumer base**, but also poses challenges for **public health**, **sanitation**, and **housing**.

questions.question: FDI in Multi Brand Retail Trade is permitted up to what limit?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**0.51**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)** in **Multi-Brand Retail Trade (MBRT)** is permitted in **India** up to a limit of **51%**. This policy allows global retail giants to establish physical stores in **India**, provided they partner with an **Indian** company.
 
• This **51%** limit is subject to the **Government Route**, meaning any investment proposal requires prior approval from the **Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)**.
 
• A mandatory condition for **MBRT** is a minimum investment of **USD 100 million** by the foreign investor. This ensures that only large-scale players enter the market, contributing significantly to the **Indian economy**.
 
• At least **50%** of the total **FDI** brought in must be invested in **'back-end infrastructure'** within **3 years** of the first tranche of **FDI**. This infrastructure includes **processing, manufacturing, distribution, design improvement, quality control, packaging, logistics, storage, warehouse, and agriculture market produce infrastructure**.
 
• There is a **local sourcing requirement** which stipulates that at least **30%** of the value of manufactured or processed products purchased must be sourced from **Indian** small industries, village and cottage industries, artisans, and craftsmen.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Single Brand Retail Trade (SBRT)**: Unlike multi-brand, **100%** **FDI** is permitted in **Single Brand Retail**. Since **2018**, **100%** **FDI** in this sector has been allowed under the **Automatic Route**, facilitating brands like **Apple**, **IKEA**, and **H&M** to operate independently in **India**.
 
• **E-commerce Policy**: In the **E-commerce** sector, **100%** **FDI** is permitted in the **Marketplace model** (where the company acts as a facilitator between buyer and seller) under the **Automatic Route**. However, **FDI** is not permitted in the **Inventory-based model** of e-commerce.
 
• **Historical Context**: The policy to allow **51%** **FDI** in **Multi-Brand Retail** was formally notified by the **Government of India** in **September 2012** during the tenure of the **UPA-II** government.
 
• **Sectoral Caps**: The **Consolidated FDI Policy** also defines limits for other sectors, such as **74%** in **Private Sector Banking**, **100%** in **Telecom Services**, and **74%** in **Defense** (under the automatic route, with higher limits possible via government approval).
 
• **Prohibited Sectors**: It is important to note that **FDI** is strictly prohibited in certain sectors regardless of the limit, including **Lottery Business**, **Gambling and Betting**, **Chit Funds**, and **Nidhi Companies**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The decision to allow **Multi-brand retail** outlets is left to the discretion of the respective **State Governments** or **Union Territory** administrations. Therefore, a foreign retailer can only open stores in those **States/UTs** that have agreed to implement the **FDI** policy in **MBRT**.
 
• Retail outlets can only be set up in cities with a population of more than **1 million** (10 lakh) as per the **2011 Census**. This is intended to prevent the displacement of small "Kirana" stores in smaller towns.
 
• The **DPIIT**, which operates under the **Ministry of Commerce and Industry**, is the nodal agency responsible for formulating the **FDI** policy and maintaining data on **Foreign Direct Investment** inflows into **India**.
 
• Foreign **FDI** in **India** is regulated by the **Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999**, and governed by the rules laid down by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** and the **Central Government**.

questions.question: The first residential university of the world, Nalanda, was established under the patronage of which of the following rulers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kumaragupta I**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Nalanda University**, located in the modern-day state of **Bihar**, was established in the **5th Century AD** during the **Gupta Period**.
 
• It was founded under the patronage of the **Gupta Emperor** **Kumaragupta I**, who is also mentioned in historical records by the title **Shakraditya**.
 
• The institution is historically recognized as the **first residential university** in the world, serving as a prominent **Mahavihara** (large Buddhist monastery) and a global center of excellence.
 
• At its peak, the university accommodated over **10,000 students** and approximately **2,000 teachers** from various parts of the world, including **China**, **Korea**, **Japan**, **Tibet**, and **Central Asia**.
 
• The curriculum at Nalanda was diverse, covering **Mahayana Buddhism**, **Vedas**, **Logic**, **Sanskrit Grammar**, **Medicine**, **Mathematics**, and **Astronomy**.
 
• The university was supported by the revenue of over **100 villages**, which were granted for its maintenance by various **Gupta** and **Pala** rulers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kumaragupta I**: He ruled the **Gupta Empire** from **415 AD** to **455 AD**. He was the son of **Chandragupta II** (Vikramaditya) and **Dhruvadevi**. He performed the **Ashvamedha sacrifice** to assert his imperial sovereignty and issued diverse **gold coins**.
 
• **Skandagupta**: The son and successor of **Kumaragupta I**, he ruled from **455 AD** to **467 AD**. He is celebrated for his military genius in successfully repelling the invasion of the **Hunas** (White Huns), which saved the **Gupta Empire** from early collapse.
 
• **Samudragupta**: Ruling from **335 AD** to **375 AD**, he is often referred to as the **Napoleon of India** by historian **V.A. Smith**. His conquests and personality are detailed in the **Prayag Prashasti** (Allahabad Pillar Inscription) composed by his court poet **Harisena**.
 
• **Chandragupta I**: He was the first powerful ruler of the **Gupta Dynasty** (ruled **319 AD** to **334 AD**) to adopt the title **Maharajadhiraja**. He strengthened his position through a matrimonial alliance with the **Lichchhavi princess**, **Kumaradevi**, and initiated the **Gupta Era** in **319-320 AD**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Xuanzang (Hsuan-tsang)**: The famous **Chinese Buddhist monk** visited **Nalanda** in the **7th Century AD** during the reign of **Harshavardhana**. He spent several years studying and teaching at the university and provided a detailed account of its **nine-storey library** known as **Dharmaganja**.
 
• **Destruction**: The university was tragically destroyed in **1193 AD** by **Bakhtiyar Khilji**, a military general of the **Ghurid Dynasty** (Mamluk era). Legend says the library was so vast that it burned for **three months**.
 
• **UNESCO Recognition**: The archaeological ruins of **Nalanda Mahavihara** were declared a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in **2016**.
 
• **Modern Revival**: The **Nalanda University Act, 2010** was passed by the **Indian Parliament** to establish a new international university at **Rajgir**, which commenced its first academic session in **2014**.

• His **Abhangs** are primarily dedicated to **Lord Vitthal** (also known as **Vithoba** or **Panduranga**), a manifestation of **Lord Vishnu**, whose primary temple is located in **Pandharpur**.
 
• Through the use of the local **Marathi** language, **Sant Tukaram** was able to communicate complex spiritual and philosophical ideas to the common people, bypassing the traditional **Sanskrit** elite.
 
• His life's work is compiled in the **Tukaram Gatha**, a monumental **Marathi** literary text containing over **4,500** **Abhangs** that address social equality, moral conduct, and the necessity of devotion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Social Reform**: Beyond spirituality, **Tukaram** used his **Marathi** compositions to critique social injustices, the **caste system**, and hypocritical religious rituals, advocating for a direct, personal, and egalitarian relationship with the **Divine**.
 
• **Geographic Roots**: He was born and lived in **Dehu**, a town in the **Pune district** of **Maharashtra**. **Dehu** remains a major center of pilgrimage for millions of devotees today.

• **Evolution of Marathi Literature**: **Sant Tukaram**, along with other saints like **Sant Dnyaneshwar** (who wrote the **Dnyaneshwari** in the **13th century**), **Sant Namdev**, and **Sant Eknath**, established the foundation of **Marathi** literature and identity.
 
• **Philosophical Foundation**: While his poetry is deeply emotional, it is rooted in the **Advaita Vedanta** philosophy, emphasizing the oneness of the **soul** and the **Supreme Reality** through the medium of **Bhakti**.

questions.question: Which of the following wildcards is used for finding the files matching a pattern?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __***.[file extension]**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **asterisk (*)** is a primary **wildcard character** used in various **operating systems** and **command-line interfaces** to represent **zero or more characters** in a search string.
 
• Using the syntax ***.[file extension]** allows a user to filter and find all **files** that share a common **format** or **extension**, such as **.docx**, **.jpg**, or **.pdf**, regardless of what the preceding **filename** consists of.
 
• When a search is performed using ***.png**, the **system** scans the **directory** and returns every file that ends with that specific **suffix**. This is highly efficient for **data management** and **batch processing**.
 
• This **wildcard** is not limited to **file extensions**; it can be placed anywhere in a **string** to match patterns, such as **"report_*"** to find all files starting with that **prefix**.
 
• In **Windows**, **Linux**, and **macOS**, this functionality is integral to both **Graphical User Interfaces (GUI)** like **File Explorer** and **Command Line Interfaces (CLI)** like **Bash** or **PowerShell**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Globbing**: In **computer programming** and **shell scripting**, the process of expanding **wildcard symbols** into a list of **filenames** or **pathnames** is technically known as **globbing**.
 
• **The Question Mark (?) Wildcard**: Unlike the **asterisk**, the **question mark** represents exactly **one single character**. For example, searching for **"data?.txt"** would match **"data1.txt"** and **"dataA.txt"**, but it would not match **"data10.txt"**.
 
• **Square Bracket [ ] Wildcard**: These are used to match a **defined set** or **range of characters**. For instance, **"file[1-3].txt"** would find **file1.txt**, **file2.txt**, and **file3.txt** specifically.
 
• **Case Sensitivity**: The behavior of **wildcards** depends on the **file system**. **Linux** systems (using **Ext4**, etc.) are generally **case-sensitive**, meaning ***.JPG** and ***.jpg** are treated as different patterns, whereas **Windows** (using **NTFS**) is typically **case-insensitive**.
 
• **Applications**: **Wildcards** are extensively used in **SQL (Structured Query Language)** for **database queries** using the **LIKE** operator, though the **percent sign (%)** is often used instead of the **asterisk** in that context.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Hidden Files**: In **Unix-based** systems like **Linux**, the *** wildcard** does not usually match **filenames** starting with a **dot (.)**, which represent **hidden files**, unless specifically configured.
 
• **Combining Wildcards**: Users can combine multiple **wildcards** for complex **pattern matching**. A search for **"2023_??_*.csv"** might be used to find **CSV files** from a specific **year** with two-character **month codes**.
 
• **Security Risks**: In **programming** and **web development**, improper handling of **wildcards** in **user inputs** can lead to **security vulnerabilities** such as **command injection** or **unauthorized data access**.
 
• **Regex vs. Wildcards**: While **wildcards** are simple and used for **file systems**, **Regular Expressions (Regex)** provide a much more **powerful** and **complex** way to perform **pattern matching** within **text** and **code**.

questions.question: Which process in the contemporary period is responsible for economic integration of countries on a global scale?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Globalisation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Globalisation** is defined as the process of rapid **integration** or **interconnection** between countries, primarily driven by international **trade** and **investments** by **Multinational Corporations (MNCs)**. ***Hence, this option is correct.***
 
• This process leads to the **free flow** of goods, services, **technology**, and **capital** across national borders, effectively creating a **borderless world** in an economic sense.
 
• The **contemporary period** has seen a massive surge in this integration due to advancements in **information and communication technology (ICT)** and the reduction of **trade barriers**.
 
• Key players in facilitating this integration include global institutions such as the **World Trade Organisation (WTO)**, which was established on **1 January 1995** to oversee and liberalize international trade.
 
• **Globalisation** also involves the **movement of people** (labour) between countries in search of better income, better jobs, or better education, though this is often more restricted than the movement of capital.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Glocalisation:** This is a combination of the words "**globalisation**" and "**localisation**." It refers to the practice of conducting business according to both **local** and **global** considerations. For **example**, global fast-food chains like **McDonald's** altering their menu to suit the dietary habits of people in **India**. While relevant, it is a strategy within globalization rather than the overarching process of integration. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***
 
• **Transnationalisation:** This refers to the process where **Multinational Corporations (MNCs)** organize their **production** and **sales** across several countries, transcending national boundaries. It is a specific corporate strategy that contributes to the broader economic integration. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***
 
• **Industrialisation:** This is the period of social and economic change that transforms a human group from an **agrarian society** into an **industrial society**. It involves the extensive **re-organisation** of an economy for the purpose of **manufacturing**. While it historically preceded and enabled global trade, it is not the process of global integration itself. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***
 
• **Liberalisation, Privatisation, and Globalisation (LPG):** In **India**, these **economic reforms** were introduced in **1991** under the leadership of Prime Minister **P.V. Narasimha Rao** and Finance Minister **Dr. Manmohan Singh** to open the **Indian economy** to the world.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **FDI (Foreign Direct Investment):** This is a major **component** of globalization where a **company** or individual from one country makes an **investment** into business interests located in another country.
 
• **Impact of Technology:** The **internet**, **e-commerce**, and **mobile telephony** have drastically reduced the **cost** of transactions and communication, accelerating the **pace** of economic integration.
 
• **Global Value Chains (GVCs):** In the current era, products are rarely made in a single **country**. Different stages of the **production process** are located in different **countries** based on **comparative advantage** and **cost efficiency**.
 
• **Socio-Cultural Impact:** Beyond economics, globalization leads to the **exchange of ideas**, **culture**, and **values**, often leading to a **homogenization** of cultures or a new **hybrid identity**.

questions.question: Two runners A and B start simultaneously from the same point on a circular track of length 840 m and run in the clockwise direction. ⇒ Distance by A = 7 × 420 = 2940 m

⇒ Rounds = 2940 ÷ 840 = 3 full + 420 m

**∴ Answer = 420 m and 3 complete rounds**

⇒ Speed of A = 7 m/s

⇒ Speed of B = 5 m/s

⇒ Time = Distance ÷ Relative speed

**Calculations:**

⇒ Time to meet = 840 ÷ 2 = 420 sec

⇒ Distance covered by A = 7 × 420 = 2940 m

⇒ Number of rounds by A = 2940 ÷ 840 = 3.5

⇒ Complete rounds = 3

⇒ = 2940 − 2520 = 420 m

**∴ Final Answer: 420 m from start and 3 complete rounds**

questions.question: Along with CO₂, which of the following initiators are essential for light-independent reactions during photosynthesis?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**ATP and NADPH**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **light-independent reactions** of **photosynthesis**, also known as the **Calvin Cycle** or **Dark Reactions**, occur in the **stroma** of the **chloroplast**.
 
• These reactions are characterized by the fixation of **carbon dioxide (CO2)** into **organic compounds** like **glucose**.
 
• **ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate)** is essential as it provides the **chemical energy** required for the endergonic steps of the cycle, particularly in the reduction and regeneration phases.
 
• **NADPH (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide Phosphate)** acts as a powerful **reducing agent**, providing the high-energy **electrons** necessary to reduce carbon intermediates into **carbohydrates**.
 
• Both **ATP** and **NADPH** are products of the **light-dependent reactions** that take place in the **thylakoid membranes**; thus, they serve as the vital link between the two stages of **photosynthesis**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Stages of the Calvin Cycle**:

 
 
• **Carbon Fixation**: The **CO2** molecule is attached to a **5-carbon** sugar called **RuBP (Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate)** by the enzyme **RuBisCO**.
 
• **Reduction**: The **ATP** and **NADPH** are used to convert the fixed carbon into **G3P (Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate)**, a **3-carbon** sugar.
 
• **Regeneration**: Remaining **G3P** molecules use more **ATP** to regenerate **RuBP**, allowing the cycle to continue.
 
 
 
• **Enzyme Function**: **RuBisCO** (Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase) is the **catalyst** for the first step of **carbon fixation** and is considered the most **abundant protein** on **Earth**.
 
• **Location**: Unlike the light reactions that happen in the **grana/thylakoids**, the **light-independent reactions** happen in the **fluid-filled space** of the chloroplast called the **stroma**.
 
• **Energy Consumption**: To produce one **net molecule** of **G3P**, the cycle consumes **9 molecules of ATP** and **6 molecules of NADPH**.
 
• **Types of Pathways**: Most plants use the **C3 pathway**, but some, like **corn** and **sugarcane**, have evolved the **C4 pathway** to efficiently fix **carbon** in **hot and dry** environments.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context**: The cycle was discovered by **Melvin Calvin**, **James Bassham**, and **Andrew Benson** at the **University of California, Berkeley**, around **1950**.
 
• **Total Requirement**: For the synthesis of one **glucose (C6H12O6)** molecule, the plant requires **6 CO2**, **18 ATP**, and **12 NADPH**.
 
• **Function of Products**: While **glucose** is the primary **carbohydrate** produced, it is often converted into **starch** for **storage** or **cellulose** for **cell wall** structure.
 
• **Environmental Factors**: The rate of these reactions is influenced by **temperature** and **CO2 concentration**, rather than directly by **light intensity**, although they stop when **ATP/NADPH** supplies from light reactions are depleted.
 
• **By-products**: During the process, **ADP** and **NADP+** are released back into the **stroma** to be recycled and recharged in the **thylakoid** during the next round of **light reactions**.

questions.question: _________ or ‘Dance of an Enchantress’ is a solo dance, performed primarily by women, in the state of Kerala.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mohiniyaattam**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mohiniyaattam** literally translates to the **'Dance of the Enchantress'**. The word **'Mohini'** refers to the feminine avatar of **Lord Vishnu**, while **'Attam'** means dance.
 
• It is a classical dance form that originated in the state of **Kerala**, **India**, and has roots that date back to the **16th century**.
 
• The dance is traditionally a **solo performance** primarily enacted by **women**, characterized by graceful, swaying movements that represent the **Lasya** style (the feminine and delicate aspect of dance).
 
• The themes of **Mohiniyaattam** usually revolve around **Shringara** (love) and **Bhakti** (devotion), often depicting stories of **Lord Vishnu** or **Lord Krishna**.
 
• The costume is distinct and elegant, consisting of a **white** or **creamy-white** saree with a rich **gold-colored** brocade border, known as **Kasavu**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kathakali**: This is another classical dance from **Kerala**. Unlike **Mohiniyaattam**, it is a **dance-drama** traditionally performed by **men**, characterized by heavy **green face paint**, elaborate costumes, and masks.
 
• **Thiruvathirakali**: It is a popular **folk dance** of **Kerala** performed by **women** in a group during the **Onam** and **Thiruvathira** festivals to attain everlasting marital bliss. It is not a classical solo dance.
 
• **Bharatanatyam**: This is one of the oldest classical dance forms of **India**, but it originated in the state of **Tamil Nadu**, not **Kerala**. It is known for its fixed upper torso, bent legs, and spectacular footwork.
 
• **Manipravalam**: The lyrics or songs used in **Mohiniyaattam** are generally composed in **Manipravalam**, which is a literary mixture of the **Sanskrit** and **Malayalam** languages.
 
• **Instruments**: The musical accompaniment for this dance includes instruments such as the **Edakka** (pressure drum), **Mridangam**, **Violin**, and **Veena**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Revival**: In the **1930s**, the dance form saw a significant revival through the efforts of the nationalist poet **Vallathol Narayana Menon**, who established the **Kerala Kalamandalam** to preserve traditional arts.
 
• **Recognition**: **Mohiniyaattam** is officially recognized as one of the **eight classical dances** of **India** by the **Sangeet Natak Akademi**.
 
• **Mudras**: The dance utilizes **24 basic mudras** (hand gestures) primarily derived from the text **Hastha Lakshana Deepika**.
 
• **Exponents**: Prominent dancers who have contributed to the global fame of this art form include **Kanak Rele**, **Sunanda Nair**, **Kalamandalam Kalyanikutty Amma** (known as the Mother of Mohiniyattam), and **Jayaprabha Menon**.
 
• **Geographical Indication**: While it is an art form, its cultural identity is strictly tied to the **Malabar coast** and the socio-cultural history of **Kerala**.

questions.question: 27% reservation for OBCs in educational institutions was provided through which Constitutional Amendment of the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ninety-Third Amendment**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Ninety-Third Constitutional Amendment Act, 2005** is the landmark legislation that provided for **27% reservation** for **Other Backward Classes (OBCs)** in **educational institutions**. ***Hence, the statement regarding the Ninety-Third Amendment is correct.***
 
• This amendment resulted in the insertion of **Clause (5)** into **Article 15** of the **Constitution of India**. This clause enables the **State** to make special provisions for the advancement of any **socially and educationally backward classes** of citizens, or for the **Scheduled Castes (SC)** or the **Scheduled Tribes (ST)**.
 
• The scope of this reservation extends to admission to **educational institutions**, including **private institutions**, whether aided or unaided by the State, other than the **minority educational institutions** mentioned in **Article 30(1)**.
 
• Following this amendment, the **Parliament** enacted the **Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006**, which mandated the **27% quota** for **OBCs** in higher educational institutions such as **IITs**, **IIMs**, and **Central Universities**.
 
• This move was aimed at promoting **social equity** and ensuring that individuals from historically disadvantaged backgrounds have better access to **higher education** and professional opportunities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Eighty-Sixth Amendment Act (2002):** This amendment dealt with the **Right to Education**. It inserted **Article 21A**, making free and compulsory education a **Fundamental Right** for children in the **age group of 6 to 14 years**. It did not deal with OBC reservations. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect in the context of the question.***
 
• **Ninety-Fourth Amendment Act (2006):** This amendment modified **Article 164(1)** to exclude **Bihar** from the requirement of having a **Minister in charge of tribal welfare** and extended this provision to the states of **Chhattisgarh** and **Jharkhand**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Ninety-Seventh Amendment Act (2011):** This amendment provided constitutional status and protection to **co-operative societies**. It made the right to form co-operatives a **Fundamental Right** under **Article 19** and added **Part IXB** to the Constitution. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect.***
 
• **Article 15(4):** Introduced by the **First Constitutional Amendment** in **1951**, it allowed the state to make special provisions for **socially and educationally backward classes** or **SCs/STs**, but the 93rd Amendment specifically expanded this to include **private educational institutions** via **Article 15(5)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mandal Commission:** Formally known as the **Socially and Educationally Backward Classes Commission (SEBC)**, it was established in **1979** under the chairmanship of **B.P. Mandal**. It recommended **27% reservation** for **OBCs** in **central government jobs** and public sector undertakings.
 
• **Indra Sawhney Case (1992):** The **Supreme Court of India** upheld the **27% reservation** for **OBCs** but introduced the **"Creamy Layer"** criteria to ensure that the benefits reach the truly needy and capped the total reservation at **50%**.
 
• **Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India (2008):** In this case, a **five-judge bench** of the **Supreme Court** unanimously upheld the **93rd Amendment** and the **2006 Act**, confirming the validity of **OBC reservations** in **higher education**.
 
• **Latest Developments:** Recently, the **103rd Amendment (2019)** introduced an additional **10% reservation** for the **Economically Weaker Sections (EWS)** among the general category in **educational institutions** and **government jobs**, further expanding the **reservation policy** landscape in **India**.
